title: How to Find a Mentor
excerpt: Most people wait to be chosen by a mentor and never are. Mentoring is not a program you get assigned to. It is a relationship you go and build.
body:
Almost everyone wants a mentor and almost no one has one, and the gap between those two facts is mostly a misunderstanding about how mentoring works. People imagine a wise older person will notice their potential, take them under a wing, and pour into them over coffee for years, all without ever being asked. That happens about as often as winning a raffle. The real thing is less magical and more available: you find someone further down the road than you, you go to them, and you ask. The reason you do not have a mentor is usually that you have not asked anyone to be one.

## Know what you are actually looking for

Before you ask, get clear on what you want, because mentoring is not one thing. Sometimes you need a guide for a specific skill, someone who has done the job you are learning. Sometimes you need a model for character, an older saint whose life you want yours to resemble. Sometimes you just need someone older and wiser to ask the hard questions.

Paul tells Titus that the older are to teach the younger (Titus 2:3-5), which assumes the structure already exists in the church if we will use it. So look around your actual life, your church, your work, your family, and identify someone two or three steps ahead of you in the direction you want to grow. Not a celebrity. Someone you can have lunch with. The best mentors are usually near, not famous.

## Ask small, not for forever

Here is where most people sabotage themselves. They walk up to a busy, accomplished person and ask, will you mentor me, which is an enormous, vague, open-ended request that most wise people will gently decline because they do not know what they are agreeing to. Instead, ask small and specific. Could I buy you coffee and ask you three questions about how you handled X? That is a thirty-minute commitment, not a lifetime, and almost anyone will say yes.

Then, if the coffee goes well, ask for another one. Mentoring relationships are almost never established by a formal agreement. They grow by accumulation, one good conversation leading to the next, until one day you realize this person has become a mentor without either of you ever using the word. Start with the small ask. Let it build.

## Be the kind of person worth investing in

Mentors invest in the teachable, and they can spot the unteachable in one conversation. If you ask for advice and then defend yourself against all of it, you will not get a second meeting. If you ask for time and then do not act on what you were given, the mentor learns that pouring into you is pouring into a sieve. The proverb is blunt: the wise listen and increase in learning (Proverbs 1:5).

So come humble, come prepared, and come ready to do something with what you receive. Bring real questions, not flattery. Follow up to say what you did with the advice. The mentor who sees that their words actually moved you will open the door wider every time, because everyone wants to invest in someone who grows.

## Honor their time and have more than one

A mentor is giving you the scarcest thing they have, which is time they will not get back. Honor it. Be on time, come ready, do not ramble, and do not turn every meeting into unloading your problems. Make it easy to help you. The easier you are to mentor, the longer the mentoring lasts.

And do not pin all your growth on one person. No single human can be your guide for skill and character and faith and career all at once, and expecting that of one mentor will exhaust them and limit you. Build a small set: someone for your work, someone for your walk with God, someone for your marriage. A wise life is shaped by an abundance of counselors (Proverbs 15:22), not by one overworked hero.

## This week

Name one person two or three steps ahead of you in something that matters. Send them a short message this week asking for one coffee and one specific thing you want to learn from them. Keep the ask small. Then show up prepared, listen more than you talk, and act on what you hear.

Nobody is coming to choose you. The mentor you want is probably one honest, specific ask away, waiting for someone humble enough to come and ask.
